items.label: f04-real-client-read
items.front: Why does the nonmember test read the issue through __realClient instead of the API?
items.back: The outsider's API reads would also return 404. Reading the row directly is the only way to show that neither sprintId nor updatedAt changed after the denied write.

items.label: f02-old-complete-gaps
items.front: Four gaps in the pre-change completeSprint
items.back: (a) sprint state and unfinished count were read outside the transaction; (b) sprint.update had no state: ACTIVE guard, so two completions could both succeed; (c) moveUnfinishedTo was never checked, so a foreign or completed sprint id was accepted; (d) movedCount came from a count() before the move.

items.label: f03-no-rollback
items.front: Why does the sprint suite opt out of the rollback proxy?
items.back: Competing operations need separate, real PostgreSQL transactions to exercise isolation and constraints; a rollback wrapper would put them in one. sprint.test.js:8 sets globalThis.__NO_ROLLBACK__ = true and setup.js:39 honors it.

items.label: f01-three-mechanisms
items.front: The three separate protections inside assignIssueToSprint
items.back: Isolation: the serializable( call (line 137). Ownership/lifecycle guards: the project-scoped sprint lookup and the COMPLETED rejection (lines 143-150). Optimistic version check: the updatedAt term in the updateMany predicate (line 156) plus changed.count === 0 -> 409 (lines 160-162). Each has its own failing test.

One 200, while the other is retried by the helper until it also wins

choices.text: It compares timestamps only to the whole second, so close edits always collide
It writes outside any transaction, so its history entry can be lost
It compares in JavaScript, then runs an update whose where is only { id }
It skips the comparison whenever the patch leaves out the title field

items.explanation: updateIssue reads the issue, compares ISO strings, and only later updates by id alone. Two requests can both pass the compare. Assignment puts the token in the updateMany predicate, so the database decides.

choices.text: 200, and the unfinished issues are moved into the other project's sprint
The sprint completes, yet movedCount is 0 because no destination was found
409 "Unfinished issues can only move to a planned sprint", and nothing changes
A 404 for the destination; the source sprint stays ACTIVE and keeps its issues

choices: 200, and the unfinished issues are moved into the other project's sprint
The sprint completes, yet movedCount is 0 because no destination was found
409 "Unfinished issues can only move to a planned sprint", and nothing changes
A 404 for the destination; the source sprint stays ACTIVE and keeps its issues

items.explanation: The destination lookup is scoped by projectId: project.id (lines 91-94), so a foreign sprint is simply not found and notFound("Destination sprint") is thrown before the first write. The regression checks the source is still ACTIVE and the issue still assigned.

Goal: compare this with the *other* writer that uses `expectedUpdatedAt`, and judge which is stronger.

Which check verifies this goal?

choices.text: isolation is the `serializable(` call (line 137). Guards are the project-scoped sprint lookup and the `COMPLETED` rejection (lines 143–150). The version check is the `updatedAt` term in the `updateMany` predicate (line 156) plus `changed.count === 0` → 409 (lines 160–162). If you can delete any one of the three and still name a test that fails, you have them separated correctly. The tests are listed in [04](04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md).

`apps/api/test/sprint.test.js` lines 96–112 set `updatedAt` to `Date.now() + 60_000` and expect exactly `captured.getTime() + 1` (line 111). `Math.max(Date.now(), previous + 1)` (line 152) picks the second argument because the wall clock is a minute behind.

The compare is not in the write predicate, so two requests can both pass it. Assignment puts the token in the `updateMany` predicate instead. items.prompt: The work passed to serializable() throws a Prisma P2002 that it does not catch itself. What does the helper do?

choices.text: It retries it like P2034, for up to three attempts in all
It swallows the error, and the transaction resolves to undefined
It rethrows the error unchanged on the first attempt, with no retry
It converts it into the domain 409 "Sprint changed during this request"

choices: It retries it like P2034, for up to three attempts in all
It swallows the error, and the transaction resolves to undefined
It rethrows the error unchanged on the first attempt, with no retry
It converts it into the domain 409 "Sprint changed during this request"

items.explanation: retryable requires PrismaClientKnownRequestError AND code === "P2034" (sprint.service.js:21-22). A P2002 is not retryable, so line 25 rethrows it at once. startSprint catches its own P2002 inside the work and maps it to 409.
